outline.chapter_title: Chapter 1: Procedural Posture and Factual Background
outline.description: This chapter establishes the foundation of the case by detailing the procedural history, the parties involved, and the specific factual scenario that gave rise to the litigation. It explains the 'Will Santos Say It?' segment on Jimmy Kimmel Live!, the role of the Cameo platform, and why Santos sued for copyright infringement and state law violations. Crucially, it outlines the District Court's initial ruling under Rule 12(b)(6) and sets the standard of review (de novo) applied by the Second Circuit.
subtopics: Parties and Jurisdiction: George Santos vs. Jimmy Kimmel, ABC, and Disney
The Cameo Platform Mechanism: How Kimmel solicited videos using fictitious identities
The Alleged Infringement: Transformation of personal videos into satirical segments
Procedural History: District Court dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6)
Standard of Review: De novo review of dismissal and scope of evidence (complaint + exhibits + judicial notice)

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 2: The Four-Factor Fair Use Analysis
outline.description: This chapter provides a deep dive into the core legal reasoning regarding copyright infringement. It breaks down how the Second Circuit applied the four statutory factors of 17 U.S.C. § 107 to determine that Kimmel's use was fair use. Special attention is paid to the 'transformative' nature of parodies, distinguishing between subjective intent and objective perception, and addressing why market harm did not exist in this context.
subtopics: Overview of Fair Use Doctrine as an Affirmative Defense
Factor One (Purpose/Character): Transformative use defined via *Andy Warhol* standard; objective vs. subjective intent; rebuttal of Santos's argument regarding original purpose
Bad Faith Argument: Addressing *Harper & Row*'s 'good faith' requirement versus modern interpretations in satire contexts
Factor Two (Nature of Work): Published status and creative nature
Factor Three (Amount Used): Use of entire work justified by parody necessity
Factor Four (Market Effect): Distinction between criticism damaging a market vs. superseding it; lack of licensing market for self-parody

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 3: Preemption Failure – Contractual Claims Against Non-Parties
outline.description: Moving from federal copyright law to state law remedies, this chapter analyzes why Santos's breach of contract claims failed. It focuses on privity issues under both Illinois law (governing Cameo Terms) and New York law (implied contracts). The chapter explains why a third party cannot enforce a contract they did not sign unless there is an explicit declaration or strong implication of intent, which was absent here.
subtopics: Direct Breach Claim Analysis: Privity requirements under Illinois law for third-party beneficiaries
outline.subtopics: - Implied-in-Fact Contracts: Requirements for alleging mutual assent ('meeting of minds') under New York law
